overview: The adaptive immune system's two arms — one that sends soluble weapons into the blood, and one that sends cells to do the job directly.
genZNote: Antibodies handle the outside. T cells handle what's already inside.

aspects.label: Overview / Core Definition
aspects.valueA: Adaptive immunity mediated by antibodies produced by B lymphocytes/plasma cells, effective against extracellular pathogens and toxins.
aspects.valueB: Adaptive immunity mediated directly by T lymphocytes, effective against intracellular pathogens and abnormal (infected or tumor) cells.

aspects.label: Main Effector Cells
aspects.valueB: T lymphocytes, particularly cytotoxic (CD8+) and helper (CD4+) T cells.

aspects.label: Key Effector Molecule/Mechanism
aspects.valueA: Antibodies (immunoglobulins) that neutralize, opsonize, or activate complement.
aspects.valueB: Direct cytotoxicity (perforin/granzyme) and cytokine release rather than a secreted molecule that circulates independently.

aspects.label: Primarily Targets
aspects.valueA: Extracellular bacteria, toxins, and free virus particles in blood/lymph.
aspects.valueB: Intracellular pathogens (viruses, some bacteria) hiding inside host cells, and tumor cells.

aspects.label: Transferability
aspects.valueA: Can be transferred passively via serum/antibodies (e.g. maternal antibodies, immunoglobulin therapy).
aspects.valueB: Cannot be transferred by serum alone — requires transfer of the actual T cells.

aspects.label: Laboratory Assessment
aspects.valueA: Measured via antibody titers, ELISA, agglutination assays.
aspects.valueB: Measured via delayed-type hypersensitivity skin tests, lymphocyte proliferation assays, or interferon-gamma release assays.
